entries.lesson_core_move: Verify additivity for a continuous-time input-output system by comparing the output produced by a summed input with the sum of the outputs produced by each input separately.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Additivity

blocks.text: Additivity is the test for a continuous-time input-output system that asks a simple question: if you combine two inputs first, does the system output match the sum of the two separate outputs? Start with two inputs $x_1(t)$ and $x_2(t)$, build the summed input $x_1(t)+x_2(t)$, and compare the result with the outputs produced by each input on its own.

Write the test in operator form so the same pair of inputs appears on both sides. The left side means, “pass the summed input through the system once,” and the right side means, “pass each input through the system separately, then add the outputs.”

If the equality holds for every continuous-time input pair, the system is additive. If one counterexample breaks the equality, the system is not additive. The check always uses the same inputs on both sides; only the way they are combined changes.
So the direct question for this section is: does one summed input produce the same output as the sum of the two individual outputs? That is the additivity comparison every later example will reuse.

sections.section_title: Checking Additivity with Two Continuous-Time Inputs

example_content.example_prompt: Use $x_1(t) = \\sin t$ and $x_2(t) = \\cos t$ to verify additivity for the system $T[x(t)] = 2x(t)$.

explanation_blocks.text: To check additivity, start with the two inputs $x_1(t)=\sin t$ and $x_2(t)=\cos t$. The cue is to form the summed input first, apply the system once, and compare that output with the sum of the outputs produced by the two inputs separately.

explanation_blocks.latex: T[x_1(t)+x_2(t)] = T[\sin t + \cos t] = 2(\sin t + \cos t)

explanation_blocks.text: Now expand the scalar across the sum to get $2\sin t + 2\cos t$. That is the output for the summed input.

The two expressions match exactly, so this system is additive for this input pair. The comparison is the same one used by the additivity test: one summed input on the left, the two separate outputs added on the right.

sections.section_title: Checking Additivity from a Simple System Rule

example_content.example_prompt: Show that the system $T[x(t)] = x(t-1)$ is additive for arbitrary continuous-time inputs $x_1(t)$ and $x_2(t)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the shift rule $T[x(t)] = x(t-1)$. To test additivity, keep the same two inputs $x_1(t)$ and $x_2(t)$ on both sides, form the sum first, and apply the system once.
Now apply the same shift rule to each input separately. Because the system just delays whatever it receives by one unit, the individual outputs are $T[x_1(t)] = x_1(t-1)$ and $T[x_2(t)] = x_2(t-1)$.

The two results are identical, so this system is additive. The comparison is the same on both sides: shift the summed input once on the left, or shift each input separately and add the results on the right.

sections.section_title: Recognizing Failure of Additivity from a Counterexample

example_content.example_prompt: Use $T[x(t)] = [x(t)]^2$ with $x_1(t) = 1$ and $x_2(t) = 2$ to show that the system is not additive.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the same additivity comparison used in the earlier examples: evaluate the system on the summed input, then compare that result with the sum of the separate outputs. Here the system rule is $T[x(t)] = [x(t)]^2$, so the key question is whether squaring the sum matches the sum of the two squares.
Now evaluate the two inputs separately. Since $T[1] = 1^2 = 1$ and $T[2] = 2^2 = 4$, the sum of the separate outputs is $1+4=5$.

The two results do not match: the summed input produces $9$, but the separate outputs add to $5$. The mismatch comes from the cross term in $(1+2)^2$, so this one counterexample is enough to conclude that the system is not additive.

entries.lesson_core_move: Verify homogeneity by testing whether a continuous-time system that maps x(t) to y(t) also maps any scaled input a x(t) to the scaled output a y(t) as part of linearity.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Homogeneity

blocks.text: A continuous-time system is homogeneous when scaling the input by a real factor produces the same scale factor at the output. This is the linearity test you use after you can write the system as $T\{x(t)\}=y(t)$.
The homogeneity check is $T\{a x(t)\}=a T\{x(t)\}=a y(t)$, with $a\in\mathbb{R}$. The system rule stays the same; only the input and output scale together by the same factor.

The simplest mental test is to start with one input-output pair $x(t)\mapsto y(t)$ and check what happens when the input is doubled or negated. If doubling gives $2y(t)$ and negating gives $-y(t)$, the system passes this test; if either one fails, the system is not homogeneous and therefore not linear.

sections.section_title: Comparing the Output for a Scaled Input

example_content.example_prompt: A system maps $x(t)$ to $y(t)$. If the input is changed to $3x(t)$, what output should a homogeneous system produce?

explanation_blocks.text: Start from the known input-output pair $x(t) \mapsto y(t)$. The homogeneity test asks whether multiplying the input by a real constant multiplies the output by the same constant.
Now replace the input with $3x(t)$. For a homogeneous system, the output should keep the same scale factor, so the new output is $3y(t)$.
Because the input was scaled by $3$ and the output was also scaled by $3$, this example passes the homogeneity check. The same comparison works the same way for any real scale factor $a$.

sections.section_title: Verifying Homogeneity When Scaling Passes Through the System

example_content.example_prompt: A system is defined by $y(t)=4x(t)$. Verify homogeneity for the input $a x(t)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a linear gain rule: the output is already written as a constant times the input, so the homogeneity test is to replace $x(t)$ with $a x(t)$ and see whether the same factor $a$ can be carried through the system.
Substitute the scaled input into the rule. The system output becomes $T\{a x(t)\}=4[a x(t)]$, and the scalar factor can be moved outside the system action without changing the output shape.
Since $4x(t)=y(t)$, the result is $T\{a x(t)\}=a y(t)$. The input scale and the output scale match exactly, so this system is homogeneous.

sections.section_title: Identifying a Homogeneity Failure from a Mismatched Scale Factor

example_content.example_prompt: A system is defined by $y(t)=x^2(t)$. Test homogeneity using the input $a x(t)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a nonlinear square rule: the output is the square of the input, so test homogeneity by replacing $x(t)$ with $a x(t)$ and checking whether the output keeps the same scale factor $a$.
Now substitute the scaled input. Squaring $a x(t)$ gives $a^2 x^2(t)$, so the scale factor moves from $a$ to $a^2$ instead of staying the same.
Compare that result with $a y(t)$. Because the output scales as $a^2 y(t)$ rather than $a y(t)$, the system fails the homogeneity test.

sections.section_title: Testing Homogeneity with an Arbitrary Scale Constant

example_content.example_prompt: A system is defined by $y(t)=7x(t)$. Show that for any scalar $a$, the input $a x(t)$ produces output $a y(t)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the gain rule $y(t)=7x(t)$. To test homogeneity, replace $x(t)$ with $a x(t)$ and track the same scale factor through the system.
Substitute the scaled input: $T\{a x(t)\}=7(a x(t))=7a x(t)$. Because scalar multiplication can be regrouped, rewrite this as $a(7x(t))$.
Since $7x(t)=y(t)$, the output is exactly $a y(t)$. The same scalar appears on the output, so this system satisfies homogeneity.

entries.lesson_core_move: Apply the superposition test to a continuous-time input-output system by combining additivity and homogeneity to decide whether scaled-and-summed inputs produce the matching scaled-and-summed outputs.

sections.section_title: Introduction to The Superposition Test

blocks.text: The superposition test is the combined linearity check for a continuous-time system $T[\,\cdot\,]$. It uses the same idea behind additivity and homogeneity: if you scale two inputs, add them, and send the combined input through the system, the output must match the same scaled sum of the two separate outputs.

Read the rule in words first: scale the inputs by $a$ and $b$, add the scaled inputs, pass that sum through the system once, and compare the result with $a$ times the response to $x_1(t)$ plus $b$ times the response to $x_2(t)$. If those two outputs agree for every pair of continuous-time inputs and every real $a$ and $b$, the system passes the test.

Start with the unit-coefficient case $T[x_1(t) + x_2(t)]$ before extending to arbitrary scalars. That simpler form makes the structure of the test easy to see, and the same pattern extends to expressions such as $T[2x_1(t) - x_2(t)] = 2T[x_1(t)] - T[x_2(t)]$.
One mismatch is enough to reject the test, so the task is always the same: compare the output from the combined input with the scaled sum of the separate outputs and check whether they are identical.

sections.section_title: Predicting the Output for a Scaled Sum of Two Inputs

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a scaled sum of two inputs, so use superposition: first separate the combined input into two scaled pieces, then apply homogeneity to each piece, and finally recombine the outputs.
Now substitute the known outputs $T[x_1(t)] = y_1(t)$ and $T[x_2(t)] = y_2(t)$. That gives the predicted response $3y_1(t) - 2y_2(t)$.

This is the same superposition pattern from the definition, now used to predict an actual output from two known input-output pairs. The coefficients stay attached to their matching outputs, and the final expression is just the scaled sum of those responses.

sections.section_title: Verifying a Claimed Combined-Input Output

example_content.example_prompt: If $T[x_1(t)] = y_1(t)$ and $T[x_2(t)] = y_2(t)$, verify whether the claim $T[2x_1(t) - x_2(t)] = 2y_1(t) - y_2(t)$ is consistent with the superposition test.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a claimed combined-input output, so do not recompute the system from scratch. Use the superposition prediction from the two known input-output pairs and compare it directly with the claim.

The predicted output matches the claimed output term by term: the coefficient $2$ stays with $y_1(t)$ and the minus sign stays with $y_2(t)$. Because the expressions are identical, the claim is consistent with the superposition test.

This is the same check-and-compare move from the previous step, now used to verify a stated result instead of producing one from a scaled sum. The only job is to see whether the claimed expression matches the superposition prediction exactly.

sections.section_title: Recognizing When Superposition Fails

example_content.example_prompt: Let $T[x(t)] = [x(t)]^2$. For $x_1(t) = 1$ and $x_2(t) = 2$, compare $T[x_1(t) + x_2(t)]$ with $T[x_1(t)] + T[x_2(t)]$ and decide whether superposition holds.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a nonlinear squared-output rule, so use the same comparison as before: compute the output for the combined input, compute the outputs for the two inputs separately, and then compare the two results.
The two sides are not equal: the combined input gives $9$, while the separate outputs add to $5$. Because the expressions do not match, the system fails the superposition test.
This is the same compare-and-decide move from the previous step, but now the mismatch itself is the result. One counterexample is enough to reject superposition.

entries.lesson_title: Testing Linearity from a System Rule
entries.lesson_core_move: Apply the superposition test to a continuous-time input-output system rule by comparing its response to a scaled sum of inputs with the scaled sum of the individual responses to decide whether the rule is linear.

sections.lesson_title: Testing Linearity from a System Rule
sections.section_title: Introduction to Testing Linearity from a System Rule

blocks.text: To test linearity for a system rule $T\{\cdot\}$, check whether the operator gives matching results from two equivalent constructions.
Use two generic inputs $x_1(t)$ and $x_2(t)$ and a scalar $a$ to write the superposition comparison without plugging numbers yet.
Use the base rule $T\{x(t)\}=3x(t)$ with $x_1(t)=u(t)$, $x_2(t)=2u(t)$, and $a=2$ to keep the first check concrete.

Pass/fail rule: if the two expressions are identical for the checked inputs and scale, the rule passes this linearity check for that test case; later steps will reuse the same template with more direct verification steps before practice.

sections.lesson_title: Testing Linearity from a System Rule
sections.section_title: Setting Up the Superposition Test from a Rule

example_content.example_prompt: For $T\{x(t)\}=3x(t)$, write the two expressions in the superposition test using the input symbols $x_1(t)$, $x_2(t)$, and scale $a$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the same as the previous tutorial: choose the two expressions the superposition test compares, but now instantiate them for a concrete rule.
For a symbolic check, the first expression applies the system to a scaled sum, $T\{a[x_1(t)+x_2(t)]\}$, and the second is the scaled sum of separate outputs, $aT\{x_1(t)\}+aT\{x_2(t)\}$.
Now substitute the rule $T\{x(t)\}=3x(t)$ into each side without evaluating $x_1$ and $x_2$ numerically.
Result: the symbolic setup is complete and both sides now share the same target expression, so this is the correct form to pass to the next step for verification or mismatch checking.

sections.lesson_title: Testing Linearity from a System Rule
sections.section_title: Computing the Output for a Scaled Sum of Inputs

example_content.example_prompt: Evaluate the left-hand side $T\{2[x_1(t)+x_2(t)]\}$ for $x_1(t)=2t$, $x_2(t)=t-1$ using $T\{x(t)\}=3x(t)$.

explanation_blocks.text: Start with the cue: this step asks for the left-hand side of the superposition test, so keep the input in the form $2[x_1(t)+x_2(t)]$ and apply the rule directly.
Now scale the combined input before the system acts: $2[x_1(t)+x_2(t)] = 2(3t-1) = 6t-2$.
The computed left-hand expression is $18t-6$. That is the output for the scaled sum, and it is the quantity to compare with the right-hand side in the test.

sections.lesson_title: Testing Linearity from a System Rule
sections.section_title: Computing the Scaled Sum of Separate Outputs

example_content.example_prompt: Evaluate the right-hand side $2[T\{x_1(t)\}+T\{x_2(t)\}]$ for $x_1(t)=2t$, $x_2(t)=t-1$ using $T\{x(t)\}=3x(t)$.

explanation_blocks.text: Start with the right-hand side of the test: compute each transformed input separately, then scale and combine the results.
Now add the separate outputs before applying the scalar $2$: $T\{x_1(t)\}+T\{x_2(t)\}=6t+(3t-3)=9t-3$.
The scaled sum of separate outputs is $18t-6$, which matches the left-hand result from section 3.

sections.lesson_title: Testing Linearity from a System Rule
sections.section_title: Verifying Linearity When the Two Expressions Match

example_content.example_prompt: Compare section-3 and section-4 results for $T\{x(t)\}=3x(t)$, $x_1(t)=2t$, $x_2(t)=t-1$, $a=2$ and state whether the rule is linear in this test.

explanation_blocks.text: Write both computed expressions next to each other so the comparison is direct.
Both sides simplify to the same expression, $18t-6$, so the superposition test passes for this input pair and scale.
Because the two expressions match exactly, the rule $T\{x(t)\}=3x(t)$ is linear for this test case.

sections.lesson_title: Testing Linearity from a System Rule
sections.section_title: Rejecting Linearity When the Two Expressions Do Not Match

example_content.example_prompt: Apply superposition to $T\{x(t)\}=x(t)^2$ with $x_1(t)=t$, $x_2(t)=1$, and $a=2$; compare $T\{2[x_1(t)+x_2(t)]\}$ and $2[T\{x_1(t)\}+T\{x_2(t)\}]$.

explanation_blocks.text: Start with the same comparison workflow, but now the rule squares its input, so a mismatch can appear from the expansion.
Now compute the transformed inputs separately: $T\{x_1(t)\}=t^2$ and $T\{x_2(t)\}=1$, so their scaled sum is $2[t^2+1]$.
The two expressions do not match: the left-hand side has the extra cross-term and the wrong scaling pattern, so the rule is nonlinear.

entries.lesson_core_move: Verify that differentiation-based continuous-time input-output rules are linear by applying additivity and homogeneity through the superposition test.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Linear Derivative Systems

blocks.text: A first-derivative system takes an input signal $x(t)$ and produces the output $y(t)=[x(t)]'$. The linearity test for this kind of system is whether the derivative rule preserves both sums and scalar multiples.
For additivity, the derivative must distribute across an input sum. If the system is linear, then the derivative of $x_1(t)+x_2(t)$ must equal the sum of the two separate derivatives.
For homogeneity, a constant factor must pass through the derivative unchanged. If the input is scaled by $a$, then the output must scale by the same factor.

Those two identities are the superposition test for a derivative system. A derivative rule is linear only when the response to a scaled sum matches the scaled sum of the separate responses, so later examples will check both identities in symbolic form.

sections.section_title: Testing Additivity for a First-Derivative System

example_content.example_prompt: For $x_1(t)=t^2$ and $x_2(t)=3\cos t$, test additivity for $y(t)=[x(t)]'$ by comparing the derivative of $x_1+x_2$ with $y[x_1](t)+y[x_2](t)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a summed input, so we check whether the derivative of the sum matches the sum of the separate derivatives. For this system, the output rule is $y[x](t)=x'(t)$.
Differentiate the combined input directly, then differentiate each input separately. If additivity holds, both paths should produce the same output.
Now compare the two results: $y[x_1](t)+y[x_2](t)=2t-3\sin t$, which matches $y[x](t)$. So this first-derivative system passes the additivity test for these inputs.

sections.section_title: Testing Homogeneity for a First-Derivative System

example_content.example_prompt: For $x(t)=t^3-2t$ and $a=4$, test homogeneity by comparing $y[a x](t)$ with $a y[x](t)$ for $y(t)=[x(t)]'$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a scaled input $a x(t)$, so we check whether the derivative keeps that same scale outside the output. For this system, $y[x](t)=x'(t)$.
Differentiate the scaled input directly, then differentiate first and scale the output. If homogeneity holds, both paths should give the same expression.
Because $y[a x](t)=a y[x](t)$, this first-derivative system passes the homogeneity test for this input and scale. That is the scalar-multiplication half of linearity.

sections.section_title: Applying Superposition to a Scaled Derivative System

example_content.example_prompt: For $y(t)=[x(t)]'$, $a=2$, $x_1(t)=t^3$, and $x_2(t)=\sin t$, compute $y[a x_1+x_2]$ and compare with $a y[x_1]+y[x_2]$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a scaled sum of two inputs, so we check whether the derivative of the combined input matches the scaled sum of the separate outputs. For this system, $y[x](t)=x'(t)$.
Differentiate the combined input directly, then differentiate each input separately and scale only the $x_1$ output by $a$. If superposition holds, the two results will match term by term.
Because $y[u](t)=a y[x_1](t)+y[x_2](t)$, the first-derivative system passes the superposition test for this scaled-sum input. This combines additivity and homogeneity in one linearity check.

sections.section_title: Testing a System with an Input Term and a Derivative Term

example_content.example_prompt: Test system $y(t)=x(t)+x'(t)$ on $x_1(t)=e^t$ and $x_2(t)=t^2$ by evaluating $y[x_1+x_2]$ and $y[x_1]+y[x_2]$ and then with scale $a=-2$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the mixed rule $y[x]=x+x'$. It adds the input itself and its first derivative, so the linearity check is to compare the response to $x_1+x_2$ with the sum of the separate responses, then check one scalar scale factor.
The two expressions match, so additivity holds for this mixed operator. The same structure should also preserve scaling, so we test one negative scalar next.

Since the scaled output matches the output scaled by $-2$, this system passes both parts of the superposition test. The mixed input-plus-derivative rule is linear because each branch is linear and they combine without any constant offset.

entries.lesson_core_move: Classify constant offset systems by applying the superposition test to a continuous-time input-output rule and recognizing that an added output offset breaks homogeneity and the zero-input, zero-output condition.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Constant Offset Systems

blocks.text: A constant offset system is a rule of the form $T\{x(t)\}=S\{x(t)\}+c$, where $c$ is a constant added to the output. The important cue is that the offset does not depend on the input, so it stays present even when the input changes.

For linearity, you want the superposition checks to work, and you also want the zero-input, zero-output condition to hold. A constant offset is a good place to see the failure quickly because a constant term does not disappear when the input is zero.
In the smallest nontrivial base case, $T\{x(t)\}=x(t)+3$, so setting the input to zero gives $T\{0\}=0+3=3$. The output is not zero, so the system fails the linearity test immediately.
That is the pattern to remember: an added constant output term breaks linearity right away, before you even move on to homogeneity or additivity checks.

sections.section_title: Checking the Zero-Input Output of a Constant Offset System

example_content.example_prompt: Evaluate the zero-input output for $y(t)=x(t)+7$. Is the rule linear?

explanation_blocks.text: The cue here is the zero-input test: set the input to $0$ and see whether the output is also $0$. For a constant-offset system, the added constant stays in the output even when the input disappears.
The linearity condition requires $T\{0\}=0$, but here $T\{0\}=7$. That mismatch is enough to classify the rule as nonlinear immediately.
This is the minimum evidence you need: a nonzero output at zero input already breaks the zero-input, zero-output condition, so the system fails linearity before any further test is necessary.

sections.section_title: Testing Homogeneity for an Added Output Offset

example_content.example_prompt: For $y(t)=2x(t)+1$, test homogeneity using input $x(t)$ scaled by $a=3$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the homogeneity test: scale the input by $a$ and compare $T\{ax(t)\}$ with $aT\{x(t)\}$. Here the constant offset should stay visible, because that is the part that does not scale with the input.

The two expressions do not match: the scaled input gives $6x(t)+1$, but scaling the output gives $6x(t)+3$. The constant term does not scale the same way as the input, so the homogeneity condition fails.
Because $T\{3x\}\neq 3T\{x\}$, the rule is nonlinear. This is the same offset-driven failure you saw in the zero-input test, now shown through scaling.

sections.section_title: Testing Additivity for an Added Output Offset

example_content.example_prompt: Check additivity for $y(t)=x(t)+9$ with generic inputs $x_1(t)$ and $x_2(t)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the additivity test: compare the output from the summed input with the sum of the two separate outputs. With a constant offset, the same constant appears on each separate output, so this is where the mismatch shows up.

The two sides do not match: the summed input gives $x_1+x_2+9$, but the separate outputs give $x_1+x_2+18$. The constant offset gets counted twice on the right side, so the additivity condition fails.
Because $T\{x_1+x_2\}\neq T\{x_1\}+T\{x_2\}$, the rule is nonlinear. This is the same offset-driven failure pattern you saw in the zero-input and homogeneity checks, now shown with two inputs.

sections.section_title: Classifying Otherwise Linear Rules with Constant Offsets

example_content.example_prompt: Classify $y(t)=2x(t-1)+5$ using the superposition test framework.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is that this rule looks linear except for the added constant. So the right move is to test the rule as a whole and check whether the offset breaks the linearity conditions.
The zero-input test already fails, because a linear system must satisfy $T\{0\}=0$. Here the output is $5$, so the rule is not linear even before we look at the other superposition checks.
The homogeneity comparison shows the same problem: the constant term stays $5$ in $T\{a x(t)\}$, but it becomes $5a$ in $aT\{x(t)\}$. Since those expressions are different, homogeneity fails too.

The additivity check gives the same verdict: the constant appears once on the summed-input side but twice on the separate-output side. The offset is the only reason the rule fails, so the classification is nonlinear due to the added constant term.

entries.lesson_core_move: Test a continuous-time squaring system for linearity by computing its outputs for summed and scaled inputs and identifying the cross-term or squared-scale mismatch that violates additivity and homogeneity.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Squaring Systems

blocks.text: A squaring system has the form $T[x(t)] = [x(t)]^2$. Before you test any specific example, you need the two linearity checks that every later step will reuse: additivity and homogeneity. Additivity asks whether the output for a summed input matches the sum of the separate outputs, and homogeneity asks whether scaling the input produces the same scaled output.

For additivity, compare the output of the sum $x_1(t)+x_2(t)$ with the sum of the separate outputs from $x_1(t)$ and $x_2(t)$. The simplest checkpoint for this lesson uses $x_1(t)=t$ and $x_2(t)=1$, so the squared sum can be expanded cleanly and the mismatch is easy to see.
When you expand the squared sum, the extra mixed term appears: $[x_1(t)+x_2(t)]^2 = x_1(t)^2 + 2x_1(t)x_2(t) + x_2(t)^2$. That cross-term is the signature that additivity fails for a squaring system.

For homogeneity, scale one input by a constant $a$ and compare $T[a x(t)]$ with $aT[x(t)]$. The base scalar checkpoint here uses $a=2$, because it makes the difference between $a^2$ and $a$ visible immediately.

Because squaring turns the scale factor into $a^2$ on one side but leaves only $a$ on the other, the two expressions do not match in general. That squared-scale mismatch is the homogeneity failure, and together with the cross-term it shows why the squaring system is not linear.

sections.section_title: Computing Outputs of a Squaring System

example_content.example_prompt: Compute $T[t+1]$ for the system $T[x(t)] = [x(t)]^2$ and simplify the expression.

explanation_blocks.text: Use the concrete input $x(t)=t+1$ with the squaring system $T[x(t)] = [x(t)]^2$. The action is to substitute the input into the rule, square the entire expression, and simplify the result.
Now expand the squared binomial. The whole sum stays inside the brackets until the square is distributed, so the middle term appears when the product is multiplied out.
So the output is $T[t+1] = t^2 + 2t + 1$. This is the baseline format for squaring-system outputs: substitute the input, square the entire expression, and simplify the result.

sections.section_title: Testing Additivity for a Squaring System

example_content.example_prompt: Test additivity for $T[x(t)] = [x(t)]^2$ using $x_1(t)=t$ and $x_2(t)=1$.

explanation_blocks.text: Use the additivity cue: compare the output of a summed input with the sum of the separate outputs. With $x_1(t)=t$ and $x_2(t)=1$, the first step is to apply the squaring rule to the combined input.
Now evaluate each input separately with the same system rule. The separate outputs are $T[x_1](t)=t^2$ and $T[x_2](t)=1$, so their sum is the reference side of the additivity test.
Expanding the combined input gives $T[t+1]=(t+1)^2=t^2+2t+1$, which does not match $t^2+1$. The extra $2t$ term is the mismatch that shows additivity fails for the squaring system.

sections.section_title: Identifying the Cross-Term in a Squared Sum

example_content.example_prompt: Find the cross-term in $[x_1(t)+x_2(t)]^2$ for $x_1(t)=t$ and $x_2(t)=t^2$, and explain why this term breaks additivity.

explanation_blocks.text: Start with the expansion rule. For a sum inside a square, compare $[x_1(t)+x_2(t)]^2 = x_1(t)^2 + 2x_1(t)x_2(t) + x_2(t)^2$ and use the mixed term $2x_1(t)x_2(t)$ as the cue for additivity failure.
Use $x_1(t)=t$ and $x_2(t)=t^2$ in the additivity test for $T[x(t)] = [x(t)]^2$. Compute each side of the check separately.

The left side has the mixed term $2t^3$, while the right side does not. This extra term is exactly the $2x_1x_2$ cross-term, so the two sides are unequal. That mismatch is the additivity failure for a squaring system.

sections.section_title: Testing Homogeneity for a Squaring System

example_content.example_prompt: Test homogeneity for $T[x(t)] = [x(t)]^2$ with $a=3$ and $x(t)=t+1$.

explanation_blocks.text: Use the homogeneity cue and write the two quantities to compare: $T[a x(t)]$ and $a T[x(t)]$, with $a=3$ and $x(t)=t+1$.
Apply the system rule to the scaled input. First compute the scaled input signal and substitute into the map.
Compute the other side of the homogeneity check by scaling the original output using the same output map.
Compare the results: $9(t+1)^2 \neq 3(t+1)^2$. The factor is $a^2$ on the left and only $a$ on the right, so the outputs do not scale the same way. Therefore, this squaring system is not homogeneous.

sections.section_title: Classifying a Squaring System from the Squared-Scale Mismatch

example_content.example_prompt: For $T[x(t)] = [x(t)]^2$, state the linearity classification and justify it from the prior additivity and homogeneity mismatch signatures.

explanation_blocks.text: Use the cue for final linearity classification: a system must pass both $T[x_1(t)+x_2(t)] = T[x_1(t)] + T[x_2(t)]$ and $T[a x(t)] = a T[x(t)]$ for all suitable inputs.
Start with the additivity mismatch already computed for the same squaring system using $T[x(t)] = [x(t)]^2$, $x_1(t)=t$, and $x_2(t)=1$.
The additivity check fails because of the extra middle term $2t$, so this already violates a required linearity condition.
Now check the homogeneity mismatch used in the same system with $a=3$ and $x(t)=t+1$.
Homogeneity fails because one side scales with $a^2$ while the other side scales with $a$. Since both the additivity and homogeneity checks fail, conclude that $T[x(t)] = [x(t)]^2$ is nonlinear.

entries.lesson_core_move: Classify continuous-time input-output systems as linear or nonlinear by applying additivity, homogeneity, and the superposition test to system rules such as derivative, constant-offset, and squaring operations.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Linear vs. Nonlinear Systems

blocks.text: A continuous-time system is an input-output rule, written as $y(t)=T[x(t)]$. For this lesson, classification is an identity-check task: we will test whether the system keeps the right algebra when inputs are added or scaled, rather than trying to guess the answer from the name of the system.

The first check is additivity. If a system is linear, then the output for a summed input must match the sum of the separate outputs. We will reuse this check whenever we combine two continuous-time inputs.

The second check is homogeneity. If we scale the input by a constant $a$, then a linear system must scale the output by the same constant. The simplest symbols to keep in mind are a generic input $x(t)$, a second input $x_2(t)=1$, and a scale factor $a=2$.

These two checks combine into the superposition test, which is the compact rule we will use throughout the lesson. In the next sections, derivative, constant-offset, and squaring systems will each be classified by applying this same symbolic test to their system rules.

sections.section_title: Classifying a Derivative System

example_content.example_prompt: For $T[x(t)] = \frac{d}{dt}x(t)$, let $x_1(t)=t^2$ and $x_2(t)=\sin t$. Compute $T[x_1+x_2](t)$ and $T[x_1](t)+T[x_2](t)$, then test homogeneity with $a=3$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a derivative rule, so we apply the linearity checks from the introduction to the same operator $T$. Start by forming the summed input $x_1(t)+x_2(t)$, then compare the output of the sum with the sum of the separate outputs.

The two expressions match, so the derivative rule passes additivity for this input pair. Now test homogeneity by scaling the same input by $a=3$ and comparing the result to three times the original output.
The scaled input gives the same scaled output, so homogeneity also holds. Since both additivity and homogeneity pass, the derivative system is linear.

sections.section_title: Classifying a Constant Offset System

example_content.example_prompt: Classify $T[x(t)] = x(t)+4$ by evaluating $T[0]$ and comparing $T[2x](t)$ with $2T[x](t)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a constant offset in the system rule, so we check whether the added $4$ survives the linearity tests. Start with the zero-input test, since a linear system must send $0$ to $0$.
Because $T[0](t)\neq 0$, the rule already fails the linear zero-input requirement. We can confirm the same mismatch with homogeneity by scaling the input by $2$.
The two outputs do not match, so homogeneity also fails. The constant offset breaks linearity, and the system is nonlinear.

sections.section_title: Classifying a Squaring System

example_content.example_prompt: For $T[x(t)] = [x(t)]^2$, test linearity with $x_1(t)=t$ and $x_2(t)=1$, then check scaling with $a=3$ and $x(t)=t+1$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a squaring rule, so we expect the output to be the square of the input. To test linearity, first compare the output of a summed input with the sum of the separate outputs.
These expressions do not match because the square of a sum creates the cross-term $2t$. So additivity fails. Now check homogeneity with a scaled input.
The scale factor is squared on the left, so homogeneity fails too. Since the squaring rule breaks both linearity checks, the system is nonlinear.

sections.section_title: Classifying Mixed System Rules

example_content.example_prompt: For $T[x(t)] = \frac{d}{dt}x(t) + [x(t)]^2$, use $x_1(t)=t$, $x_2(t)=1$, and $a=2$ to test superposition and classify the system.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a mixed rule: one derivative term and one squaring term. The derivative part is linear, so the classification will be decided by whether the square term preserves the superposition test.
The two sides do not match because the squared sum creates the cross-term $2t$. So additivity fails, even though the derivative part itself behaves linearly.
The scale factor is squared in the nonlinear term, so homogeneity fails too. Since one mismatch is enough to reject linearity, the mixed rule is nonlinear.
